forces: Trumpets, horns, oboes, bassoon, strings and continuo
performers: Marine Chamber Orchestra of the United States Marine Band; Major Michelle Rakers, conductor
intro: Handel gives the hornpipe tune to oboes and strings, then lets trumpets and horns answer in turn. The brass fall silent for the middle section, making their return in D major all the more welcome.

sections.label: A · Oboes, strings, then brass
sections.mNote: The hornpipe tune passes from one group to another

sections.label: A · The hornpipe repeated
sections.mNote: The same tune and the same turns for the brass

sections.label: B · The brass fall silent
sections.mNote: Oboes, bassoon and strings carry the middle section

sections.label: A · The hornpipe comes back

cues.title: Oboes and strings first
cues.text: The hornpipe strides in three broad beats, with oboes and strings carrying the tune. Trumpets and horns wait ten bars. When their turns come, each pair plays alone: the trumpets first, then the horns.
cues.evidence: Samuel Arnold’s full score, The Celebrated Water-musick (1788), pp. 39–40; Alla hornpipe, bars 1–17 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. The metre is 3/2. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_celebrated_Water-musick._In_score._Composed_in_the_year_1716._By_G._F._Handel_-_btv1b10072587v_(21_of_30).jpg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dance starts again
cues.text: The first section repeats, from the oboe-and-string tune to the final D major chord. The brass have their own separate turns again. Handel makes the same melody sound like three groups answering across a room.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 39–42: first section and its repeat sign. The existing section boundary marks the repeat.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fifty musicians afloat
cues.text: On 17 July 1717 about fifty musicians play beside George I’s barge on the Thames. The king likes Handel’s music so much that he asks for it three times. Supper in Chelsea begins at one in the morning.
cues.evidence: Friedrich Bonet’s diary entry, quoted in Robert King’s note for Hyperion CDA66967, gives the musicians, three performances and the one o’clock supper. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66967

cues.title: Thirty-five bars without brass
cues.text: The middle section belongs to oboes, bassoon and strings. Trumpets and horns rest for all thirty-five bars. The violins now have room for running figures beneath and around the wind tune.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 42–44; Alla hornpipe, bars 40–74 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. Brass staves rest throughout the middle section. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_celebrated_Water-musick._In_score._Composed_in_the_year_1716._By_G._F._Handel_-_btv1b10072587v_(24_of_30).jpg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to the first tune
cues.text: Da capo: back to the beginning. The D major hornpipe returns, with the oboes and strings first and the two brass pairs taking their turns. This time the opening section plays once and stops at the mark Fine.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), p. 44, marks Da Capo; the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe places Fine at bar 39. The established section boundary marks the return.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The D major chord, then the tune
transitions.how: The full orchestra reaches a held D major chord, with D in the bass. The repeat returns to the opening oboe-and-string tune; trumpets and horns rest again for ten bars. Their separate entries will follow in the same order.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 39–42; Alla hornpipe, bars 37–39 and return to bar 1. The repeat sign follows the D major cadence.

transitions.title: A middle section without brass
transitions.how: The repeated first section closes on D major. Trumpets and horns stop, leaving oboes and strings with a new phrase above the bassoon and continuo. The first violins soon add running quavers; the brass remain silent through the entire middle section.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), p. 42; Alla hornpipe, bars 39–46 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. The brass staves are empty after the double bar.

transitions.title: The winds leave the strings
transitions.how: Oboes and bassoon stop. Violins continue the running figures above a sustained bass, with viola and second violin filling the harmony. These eight string-and-continuo bars lead to the written da capo, which sends the orchestra back to D major and the opening tune.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), p. 44; Alla hornpipe, bars 67–74 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe: wind rests, string writing and Da Capo.

transitions.title: Da capo brings back D major
transitions.how: The strings finish the middle section and the da capo returns to the opening D major tune. Oboes and bassoon rejoin the strings; trumpets and horns wait their turn. The opening section is played once more, stopping at its D major cadence and the mark Fine.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), p. 44, Da Capo; Hallische Händel-Ausgabe, bars 74 and 39, Da Capo and Fine.

source.title: Handel, The Celebrated Water-musick in score (London: Samuel Arnold, 1788), pp. 39–44
source.locator: Arnold’s full score, pp. 39–44, Commons images 21–24. Bar numbers follow the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe, IV/13 (1962), pp. 44–49: 39-bar opening section with repeat, 35-bar middle section, then da capo to Fine.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor)
fields.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. A trumpet, strings with a double bass, a bassoon and a harpsichord are visible in the Marine Band’s video frames; horns and oboes could not be identified there, though the recording sounds in the bars where the score gives the horns alone.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (12 of the three suites) and the structure heard (39-bar first section played twice, 35-bar middle section, da capo to the Fine at bar 39 without the repeat) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
fields.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The structure follows from the measured level curve and the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962), which prints a repeat sign after bar 39, the Fine mark at bar 39, and da capo at bar 74. IMSLP’s tally of 74 bars (133 with da capo) does not agree with that reading (74 plus 39 bars of da capo gives 113) and is not used.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Commons gives performance_date 2017-01-29; the programme prints Sunday, January 29, 2017 at 2:00 P.M.; the official video description repeats the date. The Handel group stands after the intermission in the programme. The Commons composition_date field, 1717-07-17, is the date of the documented first performance on the Thames, not a composition date.

composer.epithet: He filled London theatres with Italian opera, then put an English-speaking chorus at the centre of the drama.
facts: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; Hamburg’s opera orchestra; Italy, 1706–10
London from 1712; 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death
British citizen from 1727; composer for the court, theatres and Foundling Hospital
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Handel was eighteen when he left Halle for Hamburg in 1703 and took a place in the opera orchestra. His father had been a barber-surgeon; his teacher Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow had taught him the organ, counterpoint and the habit of copying other people’s scores. He had enrolled at Halle’s university and worked as a church organist. Hamburg offered something noisier: a public theatre, singers to accompany and an audience that had bought tickets. His first opera, Almira, opened there in 1705, with German words and Italian arias.

In Italy he found patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Roman cardinals commissioned music from the young Protestant; Prince Ruspoli gave him singers and instrumentalists to write for. The Dixit Dominus of 1707 sends five choral parts racing through a Latin psalm, then makes them hold dissonant notes while the other voices move underneath. His chamber cantatas tried the same arts of persuasion with a single singer. Corelli’s Rome taught him what a violin could say beside a voice.
